current_episode.title: Kate Pender, Fair4All Finance: financial inclusion, innovation and big solutions to big challenges

guest.bio_context: Kate Pender started working with Fair4All Finance at its inception, initially on a part-time secondment to run the pilot scale-up programme focused on making first investments into community development finance institutions and credit unions. She then ran the first phase of Fair4All's COVID grant programme before moving into a permanent role and ultimately applying for the Chief Executive position. Prior to Fair4All Finance, she worked in economic development, supporting SMEs and small businesses to grow faster, running programmes she helped set up and run over a long career in that field.

context.real_quote: You shouldn't need blood pressure medication to be attempting innovation in financial services.
key_stats: Up to 3 million people in the UK are potentially borrowing from illegal lenders (Fair4All Finance / Ipsos Mori quantitative research)
NILS pilot: £10 million lent to 14,000 people with bad debt rates lower than most stakeholders expected
LEK research: approximately £2 billion of unmet lending demand in the UK that could be commercially viable, compliant lending
CDFIs can pay up to 70 times more than mainstream lenders for credit reference agency data on an approved loan
Shawbrooke co-investment deal: £7.5 million from Shawbrooke plus £5 million from Fair4All Finance
US small dollar loans scheme (lending under $1,000): hundreds of millions of dollars lent by 6 of the 8 largest US banks following joint regulatory guidance from 4 US regulators
Lightning Reach mapped more than 3,000 grants across the UK (initial expectation was approximately 1,500)
Fair4All Finance founded in 2019; COVID grant programme launched in 2020
entities: NatWest Responsible Finance Hardship Grant Programme

pending_qa.q: How is Fair4All Finance attracting co-investment from mainstream financial institutions into CDFIs?
pending_qa.r: Fair4All Finance secured a co-investment agreement with Shawbrooke, with Shawbrooke putting up £7.5 million and Fair4All contributing £5 million, as an example of mainstream finance partnering with the community finance sector. Kate Pender highlights what the British Business Bank, JP Morgan, and others have done in enterprise lending CDFIs as a model she would like to see extended to personal lending CDFIs. She notes that for larger organisations, the minimum deal size is a significant practical barrier, and stresses the importance of telling the story of how co-investment deals come together and what customer impact they unlock.

pending_qa.q: What challenges has Fair4All Finance itself faced as a young organisation since its founding in 2019?
pending_qa.r: Kate Pender describes Fair4All Finance as having been 'kidnapped a couple of times': first by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, which diverted the organisation's scant resources into running an emergency COVID grant programme, and then by the cost of living crisis, which again redirected attention toward supporting lender resilience in the midst of a crisis. Neither of these diversions was part of the original plan when the organisation was formed in 2019 with a clear mission around transforming financial inclusion. She draws parallels between the challenges Fair4All Finance has faced as a young organisation and those faced by the small businesses and CDFIs it supports.

pending_qa.q: How does Fair4All Finance balance impact measurement with risk when deploying dormant assets funding?
pending_qa.r: Fair4All Finance applies what Kate Pender describes as a socially adjusted return framework to its investments, looking not only at return on capital, quantum of lending, and number of people helped, but also at how financially excluded those individuals were in order to gauge whether investments are genuinely targeted. This requires grantees to provide significant reporting data on the characteristics of those they are helping, which Pender acknowledges can feel tedious to funded organisations. The purpose is to be able to demonstrate to dormant assets champions within financial services that money has been deployed with an appropriate balance of social impact and capital return.

pending_qa.q: What is Kate Pender's view on why mainstream financial institutions avoid lending to financially vulnerable customers, and what needs to change?
pending_qa.r: Kate Pender argues that when providers look at the risks of attempting something very different or serving a very different group of customers, it is 'just an order of magnitude out of everyone's comfort zone,' which is understandable but needs to change. The NILS pilot, run within the FCA regulatory sandbox, showed that regulatory support was 'a very light lift' — the team asked the FCA only three or four questions on behalf of lenders — yet it significantly reduced anxiety and gave lenders confidence to try something different. She notes wryly, however, that 'you shouldn't need blood pressure medication to be attempting innovation in financial services,' calling for structural regulatory clarity rather than reliance on sandboxes.
